analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay into retirement savings accounts for workers and pays for it with higher taxes on top incomes and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Businesses with 10 or more full-time-equivalent employees would have to put 50 cents per hour worked (rising to 60 cents, then growing with wages) into a retirement plan for each worker. Workers without a workplace plan would be auto-enrolled in a new portable 'UP' retirement account, contributing 4% of pay by default (rising automatically to 10% unless they opt out), plus a small emergency savings account they can tap for medical bills or a home down payment. Small employers get tax credits to offset the cost, and the bill raises the top individual tax rate from 37% to 39.6% and the corporate rate from 21% to 23% to cover the tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 3 in 10 private-sector workers with no workplace retirement plan would gain an employer-funded pension for the first time. Workers who change jobs could keep the same account. Workers at small firms and people with no employer plan could get a 50% tax credit on their own contributions. Workers would also get a short-term savings buffer of up to $2,500 (growing yearly) usable for emergencies without penalty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without a workplace retirement plan

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 10 or more full-time-equivalent employees must contribute 50 cents per hour worked to a pension plan for each employee not already in a defined benefit plan, rising to 60 cents and then indexed to wage growth [S2][S3].

UP retirement accounts are portable defined-contribution plans that follow workers between jobs, with auto-enrollment at 4% of wages and automatic escalation to 10% unless the worker opts out [S2][S3].

Participants can build an UP savings account of up to $2,500 (rising $100 a year) that can be withdrawn without penalty for emergencies like large medical bills, job injury, or a home down payment [S3].
Workers whose employer offers no plan, and people not employed, get a new tax credit worth 50% of their retirement contributions up to a base amount [S3].
The bill's own findings cite federal data that 30% of private-sector workers lack access to any workplace retirement plan and 52% of households 55 and older have no retirement savings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of 10 or more workers bear a new mandated contribution of roughly $1,000–$1,250 per full-time worker per year, partially offset by tax credits for their first 30 employees. High-income taxpayers pay a higher top rate (37% to 39.6%) and corporations pay 23% instead of 21% to finance the credits. Workers pay in 4% of wages by default through payroll withholding, which slightly lowers take-home pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mid-size and larger employers, top earners, corporations

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate is a real cost — about $1,000 or more per full-time worker annually at the initial rate — which could pressure wages, hiring, or prices at businesses just above the 10-employee threshold [S2][S3].
Auto-enrollment at 4% of wages, escalating automatically to 10%, reduces workers' take-home pay by default; workers who live paycheck to paycheck must actively opt out to keep the money [S3].
The bill creates a new federal board and investment fund, and it raises taxes on high earners and corporations, which its opponents would argue discourages investment [S2][S3].
Funds are administered by private investment firms contracted by the board, so fees — even 'low-fee' — flow to the asset management industry rather than a purely public option [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is large and concrete: an employer-funded pension for the tens of millions of workers who have none, plus a penalty-free emergency savings buffer — costs paid chiefly by employers, high earners, and corporations. The design has real frictions: a cliff at the 10-employee threshold, forced savings that cut take-home pay until opted out, and administration routed through private asset managers. On balance the benefits to ordinary workers are much larger than the costs, though the burden on small employers just over the size threshold is a legitimate objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on April 8, 2019, with two Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Labor Committee [S1][S5].
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers avoided a new per-hour retirement contribution, high earners and corporations kept the lower 2017 tax rates, and the asset management industry kept the retirement market as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, top earners, corporations, asset managers

industries.industry: Employers with 10+ employees (retail, restaurants, small and mid-size businesses)
industries.note: They would owe at least 50 cents per hour worked for every worker without a pension — roughly $1,000+ per full-time worker per year — partially offset by credits for their first 30 employees. The mandate is the funding source for workers' new pension contributions.

industries.industry: Asset management and financial services firms
industries.note: The federal UP board would contract with private investment firms to run the new accounts, with a cap so no single firm holds more than $500 billion — creating a large new pool of fee-paying assets channeled through the industry. The bill requires low-fee index funds and fee disclosure, but the industry keeps its gatekeeper role.

Employers can satisfy the mandate through existing 401(k)s and similar plans, so the current retirement industry keeps its business; but employers not contributing to a plan must route employee savings into state-run payroll-deduction IRA programs, a cheaper channel.
The top individual rate would rise from 37% to 39.6% and the corporate rate from 21% to 23% to help finance the new credits.
